scenarios.title: The New Kid
scenarios.text: It's your first week at the high school, and the lunchroom feels like it already has its own seating chart. A few players from the football team wave you over, but you don't know them yet.

choices.label: Join the football table
choices.result: You sit with the team and learn everyone's names. The conversation is awkward at first, but a couple of players make room for you.

choices.label: Introduce yourself to someone new
choices.result: You strike up a conversation with another student who is also finding their way around. It feels good to make a connection outside football.

choices.label: Find a quiet spot and review the playbook
choices.result: You spend lunch learning the team's terminology. You feel more prepared at practice, even if you haven't made many friends yet.

scenarios.title: Homework or the Field?
scenarios.text: Your math assignment is due tomorrow, but the field is open and the kickers are getting extra reps. You know you can't put off the homework forever.

choices.label: Finish the assignment first
choices.result: You miss some extra kicks, but turn in work you're proud of. Your teacher notices you took the deadline seriously.

choices.label: Get extra kicks in before studying
choices.result: You get valuable reps while the field is quiet, then work through the assignment later than planned.

scenarios.title: The Locker Room Joke
scenarios.text: A few upperclassmen hide a freshman's practice gear and laugh as he searches the locker room. One of them nudges you to join in.

choices.label: Step in and help him find it
choices.result: The laughing dies down. One senior rolls his eyes, but the freshman gives you a grateful nod on the way out.

choices.label: Laugh along with the upperclassmen
choices.result: The older players welcome you into the joke, but the freshman stops looking your way. You can tell he won't forget it.

choices.label: Don't join in; quietly return his gear
choices.result: You avoid turning it into a bigger scene and make sure he gets his things back. The seniors move on, though you haven't challenged them directly.

scenarios.title: Dad's Expectations
scenarios.text: After practice, {parent} says he knows you can become the best kicker on the team. He means it as encouragement, but lately every conversation seems to turn into what you need to improve.

choices.label: Tell {parent} how the pressure feels
choices.result: You explain that you appreciate the support but need room to make mistakes. {parent} listens, even if the conversation is a little uncomfortable.

choices.label: Ask {parent} to help set realistic goals
choices.result: You sit down together and make a simple plan for practice. The expectations feel more manageable when you have a say in them.

choices.label: Change the subject for now
choices.result: {parent} keeps talking about your next game. You avoid an argument tonight, but the pressure doesn't really go away.

scenarios.title: The First Rival
scenarios.text: {tyler}, the other freshman kicker, drills four straight from forty yards on the first day of practice. He catches you watching and says, "Hope you're ready to compete."

choices.label: Ask him to train together
choices.result: {tyler} seems surprised, then agrees. You split the net and trade pointers until practice ends. The competition suddenly feels more useful than personal.

choices.label: Tell him you'll take the starting job
choices.result: {tyler} grins and fires back that he'll see you at tryouts. The challenge lights a fire under you, though the two of you aren't exactly friends.

scenarios.title: The Party Invitation
scenarios.text: An older teammate invites you to a party Saturday night. Half the team is going, it's across town, and the only ride home leaves whenever the upperclassmen do.

choices.label: Go and stay till the end
choices.result: You laugh with the team until the ride finally heads out after midnight. You drag through the rest of the weekend, but on Monday people talk to you like you've always been around.

choices.label: Go, but line up your own ride
choices.result: You hang out for a couple of hours, then text {parent} for a pickup at ten. A few upperclassmen tease you for leaving early, but you still get a full night's sleep.

choices.label: Pass on it this time
choices.result: You say thanks but you're worn out from the week. You wake up rested, then spend Monday hearing inside jokes you weren't there for.

scenarios.title: The Group Project
scenarios.text: You're paired with two classmates on a science project due the same week as a road game. One partner hasn't answered a single message, and the other suggests splitting it three ways and hoping for the best.

choices.label: Take charge of the project
choices.result: You set a schedule, hand out the parts and stay up late finishing the slides. The project earns a solid grade, though you're running on fumes by game day.

choices.label: Split it and do your part
choices.result: You finish your third and leave the rest to them. The silent partner turns in something rushed at the last minute, and the grade comes back lower than you hoped.

choices.label: Tell your teacher what's happening
choices.result: You quietly let your science teacher know one partner has gone silent. The workload gets adjusted, but the partner figures out who said something and class gets awkward.

scenarios.title: The Missed Kick
scenarios.text: You miss a kick in practice that you normally make. The ball sails wide, and you can feel the other kickers watching to see how you'll respond.

choices.label: Stay after and review the miss
choices.result: You slow the rep down, check your plant foot, and work through a few controlled kicks. The extra effort helps you understand what went wrong.

choices.label: Shake it off and reset for tomorrow
choices.result: You pack up with the group instead of chasing one bad rep. A little distance helps you keep the miss from taking over your night.

choices.label: Get frustrated and rush a few more kicks
choices.result: You try to force the next few attempts, but your timing gets worse. By the time you stop, you're more annoyed than when you started.

scenarios.title: The Little Brother
scenarios.text: Your little brother {sibling} has been waiting all afternoon to show you a model football field he made. You have practice notes to review before tomorrow, and he keeps asking you to come look.

choices.label: Help him finish the field
choices.result: You set your notes aside and help line up the tiny goalposts. He beams when you take his project seriously, though your own evening gets tighter.

choices.label: Give him a little time
choices.result: You spend a few minutes checking out the field, then explain what you still need to do. He is a little disappointed, but you promise to look again tomorrow.

choices.label: Ask him to wait tonight
choices.result: You tell him you need to prepare for practice and head back to your notes. You get your work done, but he quietly puts the field away.

scenarios.title: The First School Dance
scenarios.text: The first school dance is Friday, and {love_interest} asks if you are going. You want to spend time together, but the crowded gym and the thought of asking someone to dance make you nervous.

choices.label: Ask them to go together
choices.result: You ask if they want to arrive together, and they smile before saying yes. You still feel nervous, but having a plan makes the dance feel exciting.

choices.label: Meet up at the dance
choices.result: You say you'll see them there and keep the invitation casual. It takes some pressure off, though you both spend part of the night trying to find each other.

choices.label: Skip the dance this time
choices.result: You explain that big crowds aren't really your thing and suggest talking at school instead. They understand, even if you both wish the timing had worked out.

scenarios.title: The Teacher Who Believes in You
scenarios.text: {teacher} notices your grades slipping once the season gets busy and asks you to stay after class. You have real potential, you're told, and there's still time to build a plan before things get harder.

choices.label: Make a study plan together
choices.result: You work out a schedule for assignments around practice. It takes some free time, but you leave knowing exactly what needs to get done.

choices.label: Ask for help on one subject
choices.result: You admit which class is giving you trouble and go over the next assignment. The smaller commitment feels manageable, and you leave with a better starting point.

choices.label: Say you can handle it
choices.result: You say thanks and promise to catch up on your own. You keep your afternoon free, but the missing work is still waiting when you get home.

scenarios.title: The New Teammate
scenarios.text: A new player joins the team and looks lost while everyone else gets ready for practice. He ends up beside you during warmups, unsure where to go or what the coaches expect.

choices.label: Show him the routine
choices.result: You walk him through the warmup and explain where the kickers line up. It costs you a few minutes, but he settles in and practice starts smoothly.

choices.label: Invite him to warm up
choices.result: You make room beside you and let him follow your lead. You get your own routine done while giving him a chance to feel included.

choices.label: Focus on your own work
choices.result: You give him a quick nod and stick to your usual warmup. You stay on schedule, but he has to figure out the routine by watching everyone else.

scenarios.title: The Bad Weather Practice
scenarios.text: Cold rain rolls in an hour into practice. The coaches move the offense indoors, but say the kickers can stay out on the wet field if they want.

choices.label: Stay out and kick in the rain
choices.result: You kick until your cleats are caked in mud, learning how a wet ball comes off your foot. You go home soaked and shivering, but bad-weather kicks feel a little less scary.

choices.label: Head inside and study film
choices.result: You join the offense indoors and watch your approach on the big screen. You spot a hitch in your plant step, but you don't get a single real rep in.

choices.label: Call it a day early
choices.result: You dry off, head home early and finish your homework before dinner. You feel rested, though you notice the other kickers stayed out the whole time.

scenarios.title: The Locker Room Rumor
scenarios.text: A rumor goes around the locker room that a starting lineman is about to quit the team. A couple of guys ask you if it's true, since you sat next to him on the bus.

choices.label: Ask him directly
choices.result: You find him after practice and ask how he's doing. The rumor is mostly wrong: he's dealing with something at home, and he's glad someone asked instead of guessing.

choices.label: Tell them to drop it
choices.result: You say you don't know anything and they should leave it alone. The talk cools off around you, even if it keeps going elsewhere.

choices.label: Share what you noticed
choices.result: You mention he seemed quiet on the bus, and by lunch the story has doubled. You're in on the conversation for a day, but when he hears where it started, he stops saving you a seat.

scenarios.title: The Scholarship Camp Flyer
scenarios.text: A flyer on the locker room board advertises a weekend kicking camp where college coaches sometimes stop by. It costs more than you'd like to ask your family for, and it lands on a friend's birthday weekend.

choices.label: Ask your family to help pay
choices.result: Your family agrees, though you can tell it's a stretch, and you miss the birthday to go. You get two days of coached reps and a nod from one of the camp staff.

choices.label: Save up for next year's camp
choices.result: You decide to earn the money yourself and go next summer. You make the birthday, and the plan feels like your own.

choices.label: Study free videos instead
choices.result: You spend a few evenings breaking down free kicking videos online. It costs nothing, but there's nobody there to correct your form.

scenarios.title: The Coach's Favorite
scenarios.text: {coach} asks you to stay after practice for extra attention on your approach and follow-through. A couple of teammates notice and joke that you must be the coach's favorite.

choices.label: Take the extra coaching
choices.result: You stay and work through the details with {coach}, getting several focused reps in. You improve your routine, but the extra attention leaves your legs tired.

choices.label: Invite a teammate to join
choices.result: You ask if another kicker can stay too, turning the extra time into a shared session. You get useful reps and keep the atmosphere from feeling exclusive.

choices.label: Thank coach and head out
choices.result: You tell {coach} you appreciate the offer but need to recover tonight. You miss the extra instruction, but arrive home with more energy for tomorrow.

scenarios.title: The Broken Phone
scenarios.text: Your phone slips out of your bag at practice and the screen shatters. A repair costs money you don't have, and the team chat and every assignment reminder run through that phone.

choices.label: Earn the repair money
choices.result: You trade a few weeks of yard work and extra chores for the repair. You're worn out, but the fixed phone feels earned.

choices.label: Live with the cracks
choices.result: You squint through the broken screen for a few weeks and keep your weekends free. It mostly works, but you miss a couple of messages about practice changes.

choices.label: Take a break from your phone
choices.result: You leave it in a drawer and go without for a couple of weeks. You sleep better and focus in class, though you're out of the loop on weekend plans.

scenarios.title: The Shortcut
scenarios.text: The coaches send the team on a timed mile around the practice fields, then head inside to check film. Halfway through, a few teammates start cutting across the far corner and wave you along.

choices.label: Run the whole route
choices.result: You run every yard while the pack cuts the corner. Your legs are jelly by the end, but your time is honest and you know it.

choices.label: Cut the corner with them
choices.result: You follow the pack across the grass and finish with time to spare. It feels easy until an assistant coach mentions he'll be timing the next one from the far corner.

choices.label: Tell them it's not worth it
choices.result: You tell the group the coaches always find out and keep running. Two guys follow you; the rest roll their eyes and call you the coaches' favorite.

scenarios.title: The Community Kickoff
scenarios.text: The town's youth football kickoff day is Saturday, and varsity players are asked to run skill stations for the little kids. It's your only free morning all week.

choices.label: Run the kicking station
choices.result: You spend the morning teaching eight-year-olds to plant and swing through. By noon you've chased down a hundred loose balls, and one kid asks you to sign his helmet.

choices.label: Help set up, then head home
choices.result: You haul cones and tables before the kids arrive, then get your afternoon back. It's useful work, though you miss the part everyone talks about later.

choices.label: Sleep in instead
choices.result: You sleep until ten and give your body a real day off. On Monday the photo from the event is all over the hallway, and you're not in it.

scenarios.title: The Big Exam
scenarios.text: Your biology final is Monday, and you're behind on two units. A classmate texts that he has a photo of last year's answer key and offers to send it.

authoring.ungated: Open to everyone; the unlock flags are flavor only.

choices.label: Join a study group
choices.result: You spend Saturday at the library with three classmates, quizzing each other until closing. You walk into the exam tired but ready, and every answer you write is yours.

choices.label: Cram alone all night
choices.result: You turn down the photo, keep Saturday for your friends and study alone until two in the morning Sunday. You remember most of it, though you're yawning through the first page.

choices.label: Take the answer key
choices.result: You open the photo and skim it before the exam. Half the questions match and you ace it, but the grade feels hollow, and you spend the week hoping nobody finds out.

scenarios.title: The Teammate Who Cuts Corners
scenarios.text: A teammate on your lifting crew has been skipping sets and writing bigger numbers on the log. Now he wants you to initial his sheet as his spotter.

choices.label: Refuse to sign
choices.result: You tell him you'll spot him for real, but you won't sign numbers you didn't see. He grumbles and skips the lift, and the weight room is chilly for a week.

choices.label: Spot him for real, right now
choices.result: You offer to stay and spot him through the whole workout. It eats your own lifting time, but his log is honest and he's sore the next day.

choices.label: Just sign it
choices.result: You initial the sheet without looking. It takes two seconds and he owes you one, but you know the numbers are fake.

scenarios.title: The Almost-Date
scenarios.text: {love_interest} suggests getting food after Friday's game, just the two of you. Then your friends invite you to the team's usual postgame spot, and everyone's going.

choices.label: Go with {love_interest}
choices.result: You grab tacos and talk until the place closes. It isn't officially a date, but it feels like one, and you miss every inside joke from the team's night.

choices.label: Bring them along with the team
choices.result: You bring {love_interest} to the team spot. It's loud and fun, though the two of you barely get a word in alone.

choices.label: Head home and rest
choices.result: You say you're beat and head home. You sleep great, but {love_interest} sounds a little disappointed over text.

scenarios.title: The Scholarship Visit
scenarios.text: An older teammate is taking his scholarship visit to a state university this weekend and asks if you want to tag along and see what it's like.

choices.label: Go along and take it all in
choices.result: You walk the stadium, sit in on a team meeting and eat in the athletes' dining hall. Seeing it up close makes college football feel real, though it costs you the whole weekend.

choices.label: Introduce yourself to the kicking coach
choices.result: You ask for five minutes with the special teams coach and tell him who you are. It's awkward and bold, and he remembers your name.

choices.label: Stay home and train
choices.result: You spend the weekend kicking and catching up on rest. Your teammate comes back buzzing, and you wonder what you missed.

scenarios.title: The Group Chat Explosion
scenarios.text: Two starters get into it in the team group chat after a bad practice, and it lands on everyone's phones. By midnight people are picking sides, and somebody tags you.

choices.label: Call for a cool-down
choices.result: You write that the chat isn't the place and suggest they talk in person tomorrow. A few people roll their eyes, but the thread dies down.

choices.label: Mute it and go to sleep
choices.result: You mute the chat and put your phone across the room. You sleep fine and wake up to two hundred messages you don't read.

choices.label: Pick a side
choices.result: You back the starter you're closer to. It feels good to stand with a friend, but the other guy stops talking to you at practice.

scenarios.title: The Family Budget
scenarios.text: {parent} sits you down: money's tight this year, and he can cover either your summer kicking camp or new cleats and travel fees for the season, not both.

choices.label: Pick the camp
choices.result: You choose the camp and patch your old cleats with tape. The coaching is worth it, even if your feet aren't thrilled.

choices.label: Pick the gear and travel
choices.result: You take the cleats and travel money so you don't miss any road trips. It's the safer choice, and {parent} looks relieved.

choices.label: Offer to pay for one yourself
choices.result: You tell {parent} you'll cover the cleats with savings and odd jobs. It means a tight few months, but he squeezes your shoulder and says thanks.

scenarios.title: The Angry Coach
scenarios.text: {coach} blows up at the whole special teams unit after a sloppy practice and singles you out for a shanked kick in front of everyone.

choices.label: Take it and fix it
choices.result: You nod, line up again and stay after to clean up your plant foot. The next day {coach} doesn't say a word about it, which feels like a compliment.

choices.label: Talk to {coach} after practice
choices.result: You ask {coach} for a minute and say you'd rather hear it one-on-one. The coach listens, then tells you exactly what went wrong.

choices.label: Shrug it off
choices.result: You laugh it off with the other specialists afterward. It helps you forget the yelling, but {coach} notices you didn't stay late.

scenarios.title: The Party Prank
scenarios.text: At a weekend party, a few teammates plan to fill a senior lineman's car with packing peanuts while he's inside. They want you to keep him busy in the kitchen.

choices.label: Keep him talking
choices.result: You keep him busy with a long story while the car fills up. Everyone howls when he opens the door, and even he laughs, mostly.

choices.label: Tip him off
choices.result: You quietly warn him, and he turns the prank around on the guys who planned it. The planners are annoyed with you for a week.

choices.label: Head home early
choices.result: You skip the whole thing and leave before it happens. You hear about it Monday and miss the laugh, but you got a full night's sleep.

scenarios.title: The Sore Kicking Leg
scenarios.text: After a week of extra kicking, your quad is tight and sore, the kind of ache that's worst in the morning. Practice is in two hours.

choices.label: Take a light day
choices.result: You tell the trainer and do mobility work instead of kicking. It's boring, but your quad feels loose again by Thursday.

choices.label: Ice it and kick anyway
choices.result: You ice before and after and kick a normal practice. You get your reps, though the soreness hangs around all week.

choices.label: Try a stretching class
choices.result: You find a free stretching class at the rec center and drag yourself there after school. It helps a little, and you meet a couple of runners who swear by it.

scenarios.title: The Rival's Bad Day
scenarios.text: You and {tyler} have trained together since freshman year, so you know how much the competition matters to both of you. After a rough practice, {tyler} misses several kicks and starts packing up in frustration.

choices.label: Offer to work through it
choices.result: You stay and help {tyler} break down the approach and reset the routine. It takes extra time, but the session turns into the kind of honest competition that makes both of you better.

choices.label: Give him room today
choices.result: You tell {tyler} everyone has rough practices and let him head out on his own. You keep your own evening free, but the two of you miss a chance to turn the bad day around together.

scenarios.title: The Weekend Tournament
scenarios.text: A travel team needs a kicker for its weekend tournament two towns over. It's a chance to kick in front of new eyes, but it means two long days on top of your school week.

choices.label: Kick in the tournament
choices.result: You kick extra points and kickoffs all weekend for a team of strangers. Your leg is dead by Sunday night, but a coach from another school asks for your number.

choices.label: Go watch and learn
choices.result: You go as a spectator and study how the older kickers warm up. You pick up a new stretch routine and keep your legs fresh.

choices.label: Rest up instead
choices.result: You spend the weekend sleeping in and catching up with friends. You feel great on Monday, though you hear college coaches were at the tournament.

scenarios.title: The Breakup
scenarios.text: {love_interest} catches you after school. Between practice, homework and games you've barely seen each other, and they say maybe it's time to stop pretending this is working.

choices.label: Agree and part as friends
choices.result: You admit they're right and say you'd like to stay friends. It hurts, but the conversation ends with a hug instead of a slammed door.

choices.label: Ask for one more try
choices.result: You promise to make real time and plan a Saturday just for the two of you. They agree to try, and you start guarding your weekends.

choices.label: Shut the conversation down
choices.result: You say you can't deal with this right now and walk away. Practice is the one place you don't have to think about it, and you kick angry all week.

scenarios.title: The Highlight Reel
scenarios.text: A friend who's good with video offers to cut your highlight reel. His draft looks great, but one clip is your longest practice kick with the net and the empty stands cropped out, made to look like a game.

choices.label: Keep the clip in
choices.result: You leave it in. The reel gets more views than you expected and two college accounts share it, though you hope nobody asks which game that was.

choices.label: Use only real game kicks
choices.result: You ask him to cut the practice clip. The reel is shorter and less flashy, but every kick on it really happened on a Friday night.

scenarios.title: The Friend Who Needs Help
scenarios.text: The freshman you stood up for last year catches you after practice: your best friend {best_friend} has been struggling with something at school and won't say what. You can tell it's weighing on {best_friend}, but you don't know the whole story.

choices.label: Listen before giving advice
choices.result: You make time to hear what has been going on and help {best_friend} sort out the next step. The conversation takes energy, but they leave feeling less alone.

choices.label: Help solve one problem
choices.result: You help {best_friend} tackle the most urgent part instead of trying to fix everything at once. It feels practical and gives you both a little breathing room, though some of the bigger worries remain.

choices.label: Keep your distance for now
choices.result: You say you have a lot going on and suggest talking to a trusted adult at school. You protect your own time, but {best_friend} seems disappointed that you aren't more available.

scenarios.title: The Local Newspaper
scenarios.text: A reporter from the town paper wants to profile you for a feature on young athletes. The interview is Thursday after practice, and they'd like to talk to your teammates too.

choices.label: Do the full interview
choices.result: You talk for an hour about kicking, school and the long practices. The story runs with a big photo, and your grandmother buys five copies.

choices.label: Make it about the whole unit
choices.result: You ask the reporter to feature the special teams unit instead of just you. The story says less about you, but the long snapper and holder see their names in print for the first time.

choices.label: Pass on it
choices.result: You politely decline and keep your Thursday for rest. The paper runs a story about a soccer player instead.

scenarios.title: The Relationship Ultimatum
scenarios.text: {love_interest} says they're tired of always coming second to football. Saturday is their birthday dinner, the same time as the optional film session, and they want to know which one you're picking.

choices.label: Skip film for the birthday
choices.result: You skip the session and show up with a card you made yourself. The dinner is great, and you catch up on film alone Sunday night.

choices.label: Do both, barely
choices.result: You go to film for the first hour, then make it to dinner before dessert. It's not what they asked for, but they can see you tried.

choices.label: Pick film
choices.result: You tell them film comes first this week. You learn a lot about Friday's opponent, but the birthday text you send that night gets a one-word reply.

scenarios.title: The Cheap Training Equipment
scenarios.text: You find a kicking net and tee online for a third of the usual price. The reviews are mixed, and a few say the net tears within a week.

choices.label: Buy the cheap set
choices.result: It arrives with a bent pole and a tee that wobbles, but it works. You get extra reps in the backyard all month, patching the net with zip ties.

choices.label: Save for a good one
choices.result: You wait two months and buy the sturdy version. It's worth it, but you go without backyard reps until it arrives.

choices.label: Build your own
choices.result: You and a neighbor rig a net from old soccer goal mesh and PVC pipe. It looks ridiculous and works better than you expected.

scenarios.title: The Sophomore Showcase
scenarios.text: A college near town runs an underclassman kicking showcase on a Sunday morning. Entry isn't cheap, and it's the morning after an away game.

choices.label: Enter and compete
choices.result: You drag yourself out of bed and kick in front of a handful of college coaches. Your legs are heavy, but you leave with a ranking and a coach's card.

choices.label: Just go to watch
choices.result: You skip the entry fee and watch from the bleachers, taking notes on the older kickers' routines.

choices.label: Sleep in
choices.result: You sleep until noon and spend the day on the couch. You feel great, then see two teammates posting their showcase results.

scenarios.title: The Scholarship Pressure
scenarios.text: Everyone keeps asking where you're going to college: teachers, neighbors, the guy at the gas station. You don't have an offer yet, and the questions are starting to follow you onto the field.

choices.label: Talk it through with a friend
choices.result: You admit to a friend that the pressure is getting to you. Saying it out loud helps more than you expected.

choices.label: Make a recruiting plan
choices.result: You list ten schools, email their special teams coaches and set a weekly reminder to follow up. The questions don't stop, but now you have an answer.

choices.label: Tune it all out
choices.result: You stop answering and pour everything into practice. It works for a while, but the pressure sits in your stomach on Friday nights.

scenarios.title: The Teammate Being Bullied
scenarios.text: A sophomore receiver keeps getting shoved into lockers by two seniors on the team. Today they dump his gear in the shower, and he looks at you like he's hoping you'll say something.

choices.label: Step in
choices.result: You tell the seniors to knock it off and help him gather his gear. They mutter that you're next, but they leave him alone.

choices.label: Tell a coach
choices.result: You quietly tell a coach what's been happening. The seniors get a long talk and extra conditioning, and they figure out who said something.

choices.label: Stay out of it
choices.result: You look away and finish getting dressed. Nothing happens to you, but the sophomore stops sitting anywhere near the specialists.

scenarios.title: The Family Argument
scenarios.text: You and {parent} get into it at dinner over your grades, your phone and how late you've been getting home. It ends with doors slamming.

choices.label: Apologize first
choices.result: You knock on his door later and say sorry for yelling. He apologizes too, and the two of you end up talking until midnight.

choices.label: Explain your side calmly
choices.result: The next morning you lay out what you're juggling and what would help, without raising your voice. He doesn't agree with all of it, but he listens.

choices.label: Let it cool off
choices.result: You avoid each other for a few days. The house is quiet and tense, and your head isn't fully in practice.

scenarios.title: The Rival's Offer
scenarios.text: After the respect you built by helping {tyler} through a rough practice, he approaches you after school with an idea: train together for an upcoming skills showcase. You know working side by side could help both of you, but it may also sharpen the competition.

choices.label: Train together
choices.result: You agree to share a structured session, taking turns calling out small adjustments and pushing each other through the final reps. The work is demanding, but you both leave sharper.

choices.label: Set friendly boundaries
choices.result: You tell {tyler} you're glad to work together occasionally, but want most of your training time to stay independent. He understands, though the distance takes some of the excitement out of the idea.

choices.label: Turn it into a challenge
choices.result: You accept, but make it clear you want to see who can outwork the other. The competitive edge makes the session intense; afterward, the two of you are less relaxed around each other.

scenarios.title: The Big Date
scenarios.text: You finally work up the nerve to plan a real date with {love_interest}: dinner and a movie on Saturday. It's the same night as team bowling, and your friends are giving you a hard time about missing it.

choices.label: Go on the date
choices.result: You laugh through a terrible movie and talk in the parking lot until curfew. Your friends tease you on Monday, and you don't mind at all.

choices.label: Bring them to team bowling
choices.result: You invite {love_interest} along. It's chaotic and fun and they fit right in, though you never get a quiet minute together.

choices.label: Push the date back a week
choices.result: You move the date so you can make team night. They say it's fine, but the next week feels a little cooler.

scenarios.title: The Academic Comeback
scenarios.text: Junior year has your grades sliding: two Cs and a D in chemistry at midterm. Your guidance counselor says it's not too late, but colleges look hardest at junior year.

choices.label: Build a comeback plan
choices.result: You set up study blocks after practice, trade the bus ride for flashcards and retake the chemistry quiz you bombed. By the end of the semester, the D is a B-minus.

choices.label: Ride it out
choices.result: You tell yourself the grades will sort themselves out once the season ends. You keep your evenings for kicking and friends, and the report card comes home about the same.

scenarios.title: The Final Season
scenarios.text: The first team meeting of senior year. {coach} reminds everyone this is the last season for the seniors and asks each of you to say one thing you want from it.

choices.label: Say you want the team to win
choices.result: You say you'll do whatever helps the team, even if it means fewer kicks for you. A few underclassmen look at you differently after the meeting.

choices.label: Say you want to break the school record
choices.result: You say you want the school's long field goal record. Some guys whoop, and {coach} grins and says to earn it in practice first.

choices.label: Say you want to enjoy it
choices.result: You say you just want to soak up every Friday night, because it goes fast. The room laughs, and a couple of seniors say the same thing.

scenarios.title: The College Offer
scenarios.text: A small college's coach calls and says they're ready to put an offer on the table if you keep kicking the way you are: a roster spot now, scholarship money maybe later. They'd like an answer soon.

choices.label: Thank them and ask for time
choices.result: You say you're grateful and ask for a few weeks to talk it over with your family. The coach says that's fair, and the pressure in your chest lets go a little.

choices.label: Ask about the scholarship money
choices.result: You ask what it would take to earn scholarship money and when. The coach gives you a straight answer and seems to like that you asked.

choices.label: Tell them you're very interested
choices.result: You tell the coach their program is near the top of your list. It feels good to say it out loud, and the coach promises to come watch you practice.

scenarios.title: The Senior Prank
scenarios.text: The senior class is planning its fall prank: filling the main hallway with a thousand balloons overnight. A couple of guys want to take it further and move the principal's car onto the football field.

choices.label: Help with the balloons only
choices.result: You spend a late night blowing up balloons and help fill the hallway before sunrise. The principal pretends to be mad, then posts a picture of it.

choices.label: Talk them out of the car
choices.result: You tell the guys moving the car is how seniors lose graduation, and enough people agree that the idea dies. A couple of them call you no fun.

choices.label: Sit this one out
choices.result: You skip the whole thing and sleep. The balloons are the talk of the school the next day, and you're the only senior not in the photo.

scenarios.title: The Big Interview
scenarios.text: Your college application calls for an interview with an alumni volunteer. It's Thursday after practice, and you've never done anything like it.

choices.label: Prepare like it's a game
choices.result: You write out answers, practice with a friend and iron your one good shirt. You walk in nervous but ready, and the interviewer says you were one of the most prepared.

choices.label: Just be yourself
choices.result: You show up without notes and talk about kicking, school and your family. It's a little rambling, but you laugh twice and the interviewer smiles a lot.

choices.label: Ask to reschedule
choices.result: You ask to move it to a week without practice and enjoy a free Thursday. The volunteer agrees, but the new slot lands during finals, and now you have one more thing to juggle.

scenarios.title: The Parent Who Can't Attend
scenarios.text: {parent} can't make senior night. His company is sending him on a work trip that week, and he's been looking at the floor since he told you.

choices.label: Tell him it's okay
choices.result: You tell {parent} you understand and you'll call him right after. He looks relieved, and the night before he leaves he gives you a card to open before the game.

choices.label: Ask a friend to film it for him
choices.result: You set up a friend to film every moment of the senior walk for him. It's a small job, but {parent} watches it three times from his hotel room.

choices.label: Tell him you're upset
choices.result: You tell {parent} it stings and he should have pushed back on the trip. He doesn't argue, but the rest of the week is quiet around the house.

scenarios.title: The Last-Minute Scholarship Camp
scenarios.text: A college kicking camp has a last-minute opening this weekend, two hours away. It costs most of what you've saved, and you'd miss a friend's birthday party.

choices.label: Go to the camp
choices.result: You drive out Saturday morning and kick in front of three college coaches. Your legs are dead by Sunday, but one coach asks for your schedule.

choices.label: Go to the party
choices.result: You keep your money and spend Saturday night celebrating your friend. It's one of the best nights of senior year, and you try not to check the camp's posts.

choices.label: Ask the camp for film instead
choices.result: You email the camp director and ask if they'll review a video of your kicks. They agree, and you get notes back for free, though no coach sees you in person.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Secret
scenarios.text: After practice, a teammate tells you he got his bell rung in yesterday's scrimmage and he's still dizzy and seeing spots. He makes you promise not to tell anyone, because he doesn't want to miss senior night.

choices.label: Walk him to the trainer
choices.result: You tell him you're not keeping that promise and walk him to the training room yourself. He's furious for a day, then quietly thanks you when the trainer sits him for a week.

choices.label: Push him to tell someone himself
choices.result: You tell him he has until tomorrow morning to tell the trainer or you will. You barely sleep, but he tells them, and he never brings it up with you again.

choices.label: Keep his secret
choices.result: You keep your promise. He plays through the week, and every time he grabs his helmet, your stomach drops.

scenarios.title: The Recruiter Wants Numbers
scenarios.text: The college coach who called your house a while back follows up: before the staff meeting, they want your real numbers from this season, makes and misses from every distance.

choices.label: Send every number
choices.result: You send the whole chart, every miss included. The coach writes back that honest numbers are rarer than good ones.

choices.label: Leave out the misses
choices.result: You send your makes and round a couple of distances up. It looks great on paper, but you know the film will tell a different story.

scenarios.title: The Breakup Before the Big Game
scenarios.text: It's the night before the biggest game of the season, and {love_interest} texts asking to talk. You can tell from the message it isn't good news.

choices.label: Talk tonight
choices.result: You go over and they tell you they think it's time to end things. It's hard and honest, and you're up later than you planned, but nothing is left unsaid.

choices.label: Ask to talk after the game
choices.result: You ask if it can wait until Saturday. They say okay, but now you know what's coming, and it sits with you all night.

choices.label: Call a friend instead
choices.result: You put your phone face down and call your best friend to talk it through. You don't solve anything, but you fall asleep feeling less alone.

scenarios.title: The Coach's Final Challenge
scenarios.text: {coach} has a challenge for your last few weeks: twenty straight makes from thirty-five in practice before you leave the field each day, no matter how long it takes.

choices.label: Take the challenge every day
choices.result: Some days it takes forty kicks, some days ninety. By the end of the week your leg is tired, but your misses have nearly disappeared.

choices.label: Turn it into a team challenge
choices.result: You get the other kickers and the holder to join, and the drill turns into a nightly competition. It's louder and slower, and everyone is laughing.

choices.label: Ask to cap it on game weeks
choices.result: You ask {coach} to cap the drill at fifty kicks on game weeks to save your leg. The coach agrees, a little surprised you pushed back.

scenarios.title: The Sponsor Message
scenarios.text: A local sporting goods store sends you a message: free cleats and gear for the season if you post about the store a few times. It sounds great, but you're not sure what the school's rules say.

choices.label: Check with the athletic director
choices.result: You ask the athletic director first. It turns out a simple thank-you post is fine but a paid deal isn't, so you take the cleats and post one honest thanks.

choices.label: Take the deal right away
choices.result: You say yes and post the store's ad the next day. The cleats are great, but the athletic director calls you in and you have to take the post down.

choices.label: Turn it down
choices.result: You thank the store and say no for now. You keep wearing your old cleats, but you don't have to wonder whether you broke a rule.

scenarios.title: The Sick Week
scenarios.text: You wake up Tuesday with a fever and a pounding head. Friday is a big game, and the trainer says if you rest now you'll probably be fine by then.

choices.label: Stay home and rest
choices.result: You sleep most of two days and drink everything your family puts in front of you. You miss two practices, but you feel human again by Thursday.

choices.label: Go to school, skip practice
choices.result: You drag yourself to class so you don't fall behind, then go straight home. You stay caught up, but the fever hangs on a day longer.

choices.label: Push through practice too
choices.result: You show up to everything, sweating through warmups. Nobody can say you didn't try, but by Thursday you're worse, not better.

scenarios.title: The Final Homecoming
scenarios.text: It's homecoming week of senior year: spirit days, a pep rally, the parade and a dance on Saturday. The whole school is buzzing, and the game is Friday night.

choices.label: Go all in on homecoming week
choices.result: You dress up for every spirit day, ride on the senior float and dance until the lights come on Saturday. It's the most fun you've had all year, and you're exhausted.

choices.label: Pick a few things
choices.result: You go to the pep rally and the dance but skip the late float-building nights. You get the best of it without running yourself down.

choices.label: Keep your routine
choices.result: You treat it like any other game week: practice, homework, sleep. Friday you feel sharp, though Monday's photos are full of people you didn't see all week.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Opportunity
scenarios.text: A local radio station asks you to co-host its Friday morning high school football preview for the rest of the season. It's live at seven a.m., three hours before school.

choices.label: Say yes
choices.result: You're nervous on the first show and great by the third. People around town start recognizing your voice, and you learn to talk on your feet.

choices.label: Do one guest spot instead
choices.result: You offer to come on once as a guest. It's a fun half hour, and you're back in bed by eight.

choices.label: Turn it down
choices.result: You thank them and say mornings are for sleep during the season. They pick a soccer player instead, and you sleep in on Fridays.

scenarios.title: The Graduation Speech
scenarios.text: The athletic director asks you to give the senior speech at the fall sports banquet. You'd have five minutes in front of every team, their families and the coaches.

choices.label: Write it from the heart
choices.result: You spend three nights writing about the bus rides, the bad weeks and the people who held the ball for you. Your voice cracks once, and the room stands up at the end.

choices.label: Keep it short and funny
choices.result: You write two minutes of jokes about practice and a quick thank-you. Everyone laughs, and nobody remembers the thank-you part.

choices.label: Suggest a teammate instead
choices.result: You say a teammate who's been through more would say it better. He gives a great speech, and you clap from your seat, relieved.

scenarios.title: The Younger Kicker's Mistake
scenarios.text: A freshman kicker leaves the team's ball bag out in the rain overnight, and every ball is waterlogged for Thursday's practice. The coaches are furious, and he's sitting alone in the locker room.

choices.label: Help him dry them out
choices.result: You stay late with the freshman and a stack of towels, drying balls one by one. You miss your own extra kicks, but he shows up early every day after that.

choices.label: Tell him how you messed up once
choices.result: You sit down and tell him about your own worst freshman mistake. He laughs for the first time all day, and you head home on time.

choices.label: Let the coaches handle it
choices.result: You figure it's his lesson to learn and get your own reps in. The coaches make him run, and he keeps his distance from the older kickers for a while.

scenarios.title: The Final Exam Versus the Final Game

authoring.ungated: Open to everyone; the unlock flags are flavor only.

scenarios.title: The Scholarship That Disappeared
scenarios.text: A college that has been emailing you every month suddenly goes quiet. Then you hear their special teams coach took another job, and the new staff has never heard of you.

choices.label: Introduce yourself to the new staff
choices.result: You email the new coach with your film, your numbers and a short note about why you'd fit. It's like starting over, but at least you're on their list.

choices.label: Follow the old coach
choices.result: You reach out to the coach who left and ask about the new school. The coach remembers you and says to keep in touch, though it's a different program.

choices.label: Let it go and focus on kicking
choices.result: You decide not to chase it and put the energy into practice instead. Your kicking sharpens, but your list of interested schools gets shorter.

scenarios.title: The College Coach's Question
scenarios.text: On a call, a college coach asks you a question you weren't ready for: if you lost the starting job in college, what would you do?

choices.label: Say you'd compete to win it back
choices.result: You say you'd treat every practice like a tryout until the job was yours again. The coach laughs and says that's the right answer, but they'll hold you to it.

choices.label: Say you'd help whoever won it
choices.result: You say you'd make the other kicker better and be ready when your chance came. The coach goes quiet for a second, then says that's rarer than it should be.

choices.label: Ask what usually happens
choices.result: You turn it around and ask what their backups usually do. The coach is surprised, then gives you a straight answer about redshirts and depth charts.

scenarios.title: The Teammate Who Wants Your Spot
The Coach's Recommendation
scenarios.text: The recruiter who's been talking to you calls {coach} for a recommendation. Before calling back, {coach} pulls you aside and asks what you'd want said, and what you'd want left out.

choices.label: Tell {coach} to be completely honest
choices.result: You say to tell them everything, the misses and the bad weeks included. {coach} nods slowly and says that's exactly why the recommendation will be strong.

choices.label: Ask {coach} to focus on your best
choices.result: You ask {coach} to talk about your leg and your work ethic and skip the rough patch. The coach agrees, but you can tell it isn't the conversation they hoped for.

choices.label: Leave it entirely to {coach}
choices.result: You say it's {coach}'s call and you trust whatever gets said. The coach looks a little surprised, then says thanks for the trust.

scenarios.title: The Final Rivalry
scenarios.text: With the final stretch of senior season approaching, {tyler} is still the rival who knows exactly how to get under your skin. A few teammates bring up the competition between you, and you have to decide what you want these last weeks to mean.

choices.label: Let the rivalry fuel you
choices.result: You channel the tension into a focused routine and keep your attention on the work in front of you. The edge gives you energy, but it is harder to switch off afterward.

choices.label: Make peace before it ends
choices.result: You speak with {tyler} privately and say you don't want the season to end with bitterness. The conversation doesn't erase the past, but it eases the tension and gives you some perspective.

choices.label: Avoid the conversation
choices.result: You keep your distance and let the others talk. It saves you from another uncomfortable exchange, but the unresolved tension follows you through the week.

scenarios.title: The Teammate Who Remembers
scenarios.text: A classmate you stood up for as a freshman recognizes you in the hallway. He says he still remembers that you helped when older students hid his gear, and asks how you've been handling the pressure this year.

choices.label: Catch up with him
choices.result: You make time to listen and share a little about your own year. The conversation lifts both your spirits, even though you arrive at your next stop feeling behind.

choices.label: Offer practical advice
choices.result: You talk through ways to handle team pressure and school responsibilities. He leaves with a plan, and you feel good about helping, though the advice takes more out of you than expected.

choices.label: Keep it brief
choices.result: You give him a friendly greeting and say you have to get moving. You protect your time, but the quick exchange feels a little distant after he made the effort to find you.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Recruiter
scenarios.text: You've been hoping to hear from the big programs, but the recruiter who shows up at practice is from a small college two hours away. The coach watched every rep and wants to talk.

choices.label: Give them your full attention
choices.result: You sit down with the coach for half an hour and ask real questions about the program. You leave impressed by how much they already know about you.

choices.label: Be polite, but keep waiting
choices.result: You thank the coach and say you're still waiting to hear from a few other schools. The coach says the door is open, and you wonder if you just closed it a little.

choices.label: Ask how you'd fit right away
choices.result: You ask whether you'd compete for the job as a freshman. The answer is yes, and suddenly the small school looks a lot bigger.

scenarios.title: The Wrong Locker
scenarios.text: You open your locker and find someone else's books inside. An older student steps over, says you took his locker, and starts raising his voice as other students watch.

choices.label: Stay calm and sort it out
choices.result: You explain which locker number is on your schedule and offer to check with the office together. The mix-up gets cleared up without a scene, and the older student backs off.

choices.label: Snap back at him
choices.result: You tell him to prove it and raise your voice too. He eventually walks away, but the hallway turns into an audience and the disagreement follows you into class.

scenarios.title: The Open Gym
scenarios.text: The school opens the gym after classes, and a few players are setting up a kicking station. You have time to join them, but you also have homework and a chance to take the afternoon easy.

choices.label: Join the kicking session
choices.result: You take turns kicking into the practice net and get pointers on your approach. The extra reps sharpen your routine, though you get home later than planned.

choices.label: Save the afternoon
choices.result: You head home instead and get your assignments finished before relaxing. Your legs feel fresh the next day, but you miss a chance to get extra work in.

scenarios.title: The First Group Chat
scenarios.text: A group chat starts making fun of a teammate after an awkward moment at practice, and the jokes keep piling up. You know the teammate will probably see the messages, and everyone in the chat can see what you do next.

choices.label: Tell them to knock it off
choices.result: You say the jokes have gone too far and ask the group to leave the teammate alone. A few people go quiet, but you feel better knowing you didn't let it slide.

choices.label: Check in privately
choices.result: You message the teammate directly and let them know you saw the chat and don't agree with it. They appreciate hearing from you, even though the group chat carries on without you stepping in publicly.

choices.label: Join in with the jokes
choices.result: You add a joke of your own, and the chat fills with laughing reactions. It feels easy to fit in for the moment, but the teammate stops talking when you see them at practice.

scenarios.title: The Family Road Trip
scenarios.text: Your family has planned a road trip for the same weekend as your first kicking clinic. {parent} says the trip matters to everyone, while the clinic could give you a chance to learn from experienced kickers.

choices.label: Take the family trip
choices.result: You go on the trip and enjoy having everyone together without thinking about practice for a couple of days. You miss the clinic, but {parent} appreciates that you made the family plans a priority.

choices.label: Attend the kicking clinic
choices.result: You explain why the clinic matters and travel there while your family heads out. You get valuable instruction and several focused reps, though you miss the shared trip and {parent} is disappointed.

choices.label: Work out a split weekend
choices.result: You attend part of the clinic, then meet your family for the rest of the trip. You don't get the full clinic experience, but you still learn a few things and make time for everyone.

scenarios.title: The New Equipment
scenarios.text: Your kicking cleats are splitting at the seam. The pair everyone on the team wants costs more than your family usually spends on gear in a year.

choices.label: Earn the money yourself
choices.result: You mow lawns and walk a neighbor's dog for three weekends until you can cover most of the cost. The new cleats take a while, but every time you lace them up, they feel earned.

choices.label: Ask for the expensive pair
choices.result: You make your case at dinner, and your family stretches the budget to get them before Friday. They feel great on your foot, though you notice nobody mentions the price again.

scenarios.title: The Substitute Holder
scenarios.text: Your usual holder, {holder}, is unavailable for part of practice, and a backup is filling in. The backup is still learning how to place the ball and time the snap, so you can either help them get comfortable or stick to your own routine.

choices.label: Help train the backup holder
choices.result: You slow things down and work through the snap, spot, and timing together. It takes time away from your own kicks, but the backup starts getting the ball down more consistently.

choices.label: Stick with your own routine
choices.result: You ask to keep your reps moving and let the coaches handle the backup's instruction. You get more kicks in, but the backup is still unsure about the timing when practice ends.

scenarios.title: The First Volunteer Day
scenarios.text: A community volunteer day is coming up, and organizers need help setting up a youth sports field before the weekend games. You can commit to the full morning or stop by for a shorter shift around your other plans.

choices.label: Commit to the full morning
choices.result: You spend the morning moving equipment, setting up cones, and getting the field ready. You're worn out by the end, but the organizers are grateful you stayed until the work was done.

choices.label: Help for a shorter shift
choices.result: You arrive early, help unload supplies, and stay until the main setup is finished. You have time for the rest of your day, though you leave before the final cleanup.

scenarios.title: The First Bad Grade
scenarios.text: Your first big algebra test comes back with a D circled in red. {teacher} hands it back without a word, but there's a note at the bottom: "Come see me."

choices.label: Go see {teacher} after class
choices.result: You show up after the last bell, and {teacher} walks you through every mistake. It eats your free period for two weeks, but the next quiz comes back a B.

choices.label: Blame the test and move on
choices.result: You tell your friends the test was unfair and shove it in your locker. It's easy to forget about, right up until the next test covers the same material.

scenarios.title: The Practice Playlist
scenarios.text: The upperclassmen control the speaker at practice, and the freshmen are sick of hearing the same playlist every day. A few of them ask you to bring it up, since you get along with everybody.

choices.label: Pitch a shared playlist
choices.result: You suggest every class adds a few songs to one rotation. The seniors grumble, then agree, and warmups suddenly feel like they belong to everyone.

choices.label: Leave it alone
choices.result: You tell them it isn't worth the trouble, and the same playlist keeps blasting. Nothing changes, but nobody's annoyed with you either.

scenarios.title: The First Time You're Recognized
scenarios.text: After a kick that gets the sideline cheering, a school photographer asks for a quick picture and a few words about it. Teammates nearby are still celebrating, and you have to decide how to handle the attention.

choices.label: Give the team the credit
choices.result: You mention the snap, the hold, and the teammates who helped you prepare. The photographer gets a good quote, and your teammates appreciate that you included them in the moment.

choices.label: Enjoy the attention
choices.result: You smile for the camera and talk about how much the kick means to you. The attention feels great, though a couple of teammates think you could have mentioned the work everyone put in.

choices.label: Keep it low-key
choices.result: You tell the photographer it was just one kick and that there's plenty of work left to do. You avoid the spotlight, but some classmates read your answer as brushing off a moment they were excited to celebrate.

scenarios.title: The New Quarterback
scenarios.text: A transfer quarterback named Jonah Pike joins the team, and on his first day he boots a few kickoffs for fun, deep into the end zone. The whole locker room is talking about it, and {coach} jokes that you might have competition.

choices.label: Welcome him to the team
choices.result: You introduce yourself, show him where the specialists warm up and joke that kickoffs are still yours. Jonah laughs, and by Friday he's saving you a seat on the bus.

choices.label: Show him whose job it is
choices.result: You stay late and blast kickoff after kickoff while he watches. Your leg feels great, but Jonah starts keeping score, and the locker room picks sides.

scenarios.title: The Missed Team Bus
scenarios.text: Your alarm doesn't go off, and you wake up to six missed texts: the bus to the away game left ten minutes ago. You can still make warmups if you find a ride now.

choices.label: Call {coach} and own it
choices.result: You call {coach} first and admit you overslept, then get {parent} to drive you. You make warmups with minutes to spare, and the coach says the call is what counted.

choices.label: Find a ride and slip in
choices.result: You get {parent} to drive you and jog into warmups like nothing happened. Nobody says much, but you spend the whole night wondering who noticed.

choices.label: Blame the schedule
choices.result: You text the team chat that nobody told you the bus time changed. A few guys back you up, but a teammate posts the reminder from yesterday, and the chat goes quiet.

scenarios.title: The Secret Training Session
scenarios.text: A retired kicking coach in the next town offers Sunday morning sessions. They're good, people say, but they cost real money, and you'd be paying out of your own savings.

choices.label: Pay for the sessions
choices.result: You empty your savings jar and drive out every Sunday. It's expensive and exhausting, but your kickoffs start hanging in the air longer.

choices.label: Keep your savings
choices.result: You decide the money matters more right now and stick to your usual routine. Your Sundays stay free, though you wonder what you're missing.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Excuse
scenarios.text: A teammate skipped Tuesday's practice to go to a concert. Now he wants you to tell the coaches he was with you at a study session.

choices.label: Tell him you won't lie
choices.result: You tell him you won't cover for him, but you won't bring it up either. He's annoyed, and he ends up running extra laps when the coaches find out anyway.

choices.label: Tell the coaches the truth
choices.result: When a coach asks you directly, you tell the truth. He has to sit out the first quarter on Friday, and a few teammates call you a snitch.

choices.label: Back up his story
choices.result: You tell the coaches he was studying with you. It works and he owes you big, but you flinch every time someone mentions that concert.

scenarios.title: The Summer Job Interview
scenarios.text: The pizza place downtown is hiring for the summer, and the manager offers you a job on the spot: twenty hours a week, nights and weekends. It's real money, but summer is when kickers make their biggest jump.

choices.label: Take every shift
choices.result: You take the full schedule and come home smelling like pizza most nights. Your savings grow fast, though your kicking bag sits in the closet more than you'd like.

choices.label: Turn it down to train
choices.result: You tell the manager thanks, but this summer is for football. You kick almost every morning and lift every afternoon, and your wallet stays empty.

choices.label: Ask for hours around training
choices.result: You ask for evenings only so your mornings stay free for kicking. The manager agrees to fifteen hours, and you spend the summer tired but juggling both.

scenarios.title: The Social Media Challenge
scenarios.text: A kicking challenge is going around online: hit the crossbar from forty yards on video. Your friends say you have to try it, and everyone's posting something.

choices.label: Film the crossbar challenge
choices.result: It takes thirty-one tries, but you finally ring the crossbar on camera. The clip blows up at school, and you're sore from chasing balls all afternoon.

choices.label: Post your real training
choices.result: You post a short clip of your morning routine and a note about what you're working on. It gets fewer likes, but a couple of college kickers comment with tips.

scenarios.title: The Coach Who Remembers
scenarios.text: A college special teams coach is watching practice, and afterward he remembers you from a youth kicking clinic years ago. He asks how your season is really going.

choices.label: Give him an honest update
choices.result: You tell him where you're strong and where you still miss, including the hook you're working out. He nods, writes something down and tells you to keep him posted.

choices.label: Talk up your numbers
choices.result: You round your long make up to fifty and leave out the misses. He seems impressed and asks for film of those kicks, which you don't have.

choices.label: Ask what he'd fix
choices.result: You ask what college coaches look for and what he'd change in your approach. He spends ten minutes on your plant foot, and you leave with homework instead of a business card.

scenarios.title: The Leadership Nomination
scenarios.text: {teacher} nominates you for the school's student leadership program: Tuesday afternoon meetings, a service project and a spot at the spring assembly. It's an honor, but Tuesday is your extra lifting day.

choices.label: Accept the nomination
choices.result: You give up the Tuesday lift and end up running the food drive committee. It's more work than you expected, but you learn how to get a room full of people moving.

choices.label: Keep your lifting day
choices.result: You thank {teacher} and explain that football fills your schedule. The nomination goes to someone else, and you keep your Tuesday reps.

scenarios.title: The Cheap Private Lesson
scenarios.text: A guy at the park is offering private kicking lessons for half what anyone else charges. He talks a big game about college kickers he's trained, but nobody you know has heard of him.

choices.label: Check him out first
choices.result: You look up his name, ask for references and watch one of his sessions from the bleachers. He's real but basic, and you book two lessons knowing exactly what you're getting.

choices.label: Book lessons right away
choices.result: You sign up on the spot and spend three evenings on his drills. He pushes you hard on a new leg swing, and your hip is sore by the end of the week.

choices.label: Ask {coach} about him
choices.result: {coach} has never heard of him and offers to stay after practice for extra reps instead. It's free, though the drills are ones you already know.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Big Opportunity
scenarios.text: The coaches can send one kicker to a regional specialist showcase this spring, and it's between you and a sophomore punter who has practiced next to you all year. The day before they decide, he asks you to watch his approach and tell him what you see.

choices.label: Help him fix his approach
choices.result: You point out his stutter step and show him how to set his marks. He kicks the best he has all year and gets the showcase spot, then thanks you in front of the whole special teams unit.

choices.label: Steer him wrong
choices.result: You tell him to lengthen his approach, knowing it will throw off his timing. You get the showcase spot, but every time he walks past you at practice, your stomach turns.

scenarios.title: The College Camp Conflict
scenarios.text: Two college camps invite you for the same summer weekend: one at the school you've dreamed about since you were a kid, and one where the special teams coach has emailed you every month.

choices.label: Go where they want you
choices.result: You pick the school that's been recruiting you hardest. The coach works with you all weekend and talks about a roster spot, though you can't stop checking the other camp's photos online.

choices.label: Call both coaches first
choices.result: You call both staffs, explain the conflict and ask whether either has another date. The dream school offers a later session, and the other coach tells you he respects that you called.

scenarios.title: The Starting Job Is in Question
scenarios.text: After two shaky weeks, {coach} starts splitting first-team practice reps between you and the backup kicker. Nobody has said the job is open, but everyone has noticed.

choices.label: Ask {coach} what to fix
choices.result: You stay after practice and ask what {coach} needs to see from you. The answer is blunt: quicker get-off, fewer hooks. You have a list and a deadline.

choices.label: Tell {coach} it isn't fair
choices.result: You tell {coach} that two bad weeks shouldn't cost you reps after everything you've done. The conversation gets tense, and you leave fired up but no surer of where you stand.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Family Problem
scenarios.text: A teammate you lift with has been showing up late and exhausted. After practice he admits his mom lost her job and he's been working nights to help with rent.

choices.label: Help him quietly
choices.result: You start giving him rides and sharing your lunch without making a thing of it. He never says much, but he's on time all week.

choices.label: Bring {coach} in, with his OK
choices.result: You convince him to let you tell {coach}. The coach quietly finds him a school job with set hours, and within a couple of weeks he looks like himself again.

scenarios.title: The Recruiter's Social Media Search
scenarios.text: A college recruiter mentions, almost casually, that their staff looks through every recruit's social media. You remember an old post from freshman year making fun of another team's kicker, still sitting near the top of your page.

choices.label: Delete it and own it
choices.result: You take the post down and message the recruiter that it was dumb and you've grown up since. The reply is short, but it ends with 'appreciate you saying so.'

choices.label: Bury it under a flashy clip
choices.result: You pin a slick new highlight to the top of your page, edited so a practice kick looks like it came under the lights. The old post slides out of sight, but now there's something new you'd have to explain.

scenarios.title: The Injury You Don't Mention
scenarios.text: A sharp pain has been catching in your kicking hip for two weeks, worst on the follow-through. You haven't told anyone, and Friday's game is the one everyone has circled.

choices.label: Tell the athletic trainer
choices.result: You walk into the training room and describe exactly where it hurts. The trainer cuts your kicking reps in half for a week and gives you a stretching routine, and the coaches start asking how you feel every day.

choices.label: Quietly cut back your reps
choices.result: You skip your extra kicks after practice and ice at home without saying why. The pain eases a little, but you're behind on your work and hoping nobody notices.

choices.label: Push through it
choices.result: You keep your full routine and wince through the follow-through when nobody's looking. Your leg still feels strong, but every kick ends with a flash of pain you can't ignore.

scenarios.title: The Hallway Favor
scenarios.text: After you calmly settled that locker mix-up as a freshman, a younger student approaches you in the hallway with a similar problem: an older student keeps telling them they don't belong in a certain part of the team area. They ask what you would do.

choices.label: Walk them through it
choices.result: You help the student explain the situation clearly and offer to go with them to the office or coach. It costs part of your break, but they leave with a plan and more confidence.

choices.label: Point them to an adult
choices.result: You encourage them to speak with a coach or school staff member who can sort out the issue properly. You keep your own schedule on track, though the student has to take the next step without you beside them.

scenarios.title: The College Coach's Criticism
scenarios.text: At a college camp, a special teams coach watches you kick and doesn't sugarcoat it: your get-off is slow, your misses all drift left, and you look nervous. He says he'll check back in a year.

choices.label: Ask him to show you
choices.result: You ask him to walk you through the film right there. It stings to watch your misses in slow motion, but you leave with two drills and a clear idea of what he wants to see.

choices.label: Use it as fuel
choices.result: You nod, say thanks and replay every word on the drive home. For weeks you kick with a chip on your shoulder, faster and angrier, though your aim gets streaky.

scenarios.title: The Scholarship Rumor
scenarios.text: A rumor races through school that a big college is about to offer you a scholarship. Teammates are congratulating you, and a few people want you to post about it, but nobody from that school has actually called.

choices.label: Find out what's true
choices.result: You email the school's special teams coach and ask, politely, where you stand. The answer is honest: you're on their list, nothing more yet. It's less exciting, but it's real.

choices.label: Ride the wave
choices.result: You post a cryptic 'big things coming' with the school's colors in the background. Your phone blows up for a week, and you try not to think about what happens when the offer doesn't come.

scenarios.title: The First Paycheck
scenarios.text: Your first paycheck from your weekend job is more money than you've ever held. The same week, you hear {parent} on the phone about a car repair the family can't really afford.

choices.label: Save it for training
choices.result: You open a savings account and set the money aside for a kicking camp next summer. It feels grown-up, though you can't stop thinking about the phone call.

choices.label: Give it to {parent}
choices.result: You hand him the envelope at dinner. He tries to refuse, then hugs you a little too long, and the car gets fixed by the weekend.

scenarios.title: The Senior Kicker's Advice
scenarios.text: The team's senior punter has kicked on this field for four years. After practice he offers to show you the little things he's learned: how the wind swirls at the south end, how he settles his breathing before a big kick.

choices.label: Spend the week learning from him
choices.result: You stay late every day and fill a notebook with his tips. Some of it is superstition, but the wind notes alone are worth it.

choices.label: Thank him and stick to your routine
choices.result: You thank him and keep your own approach. Your routine stays tight, though you notice him sharing the same tips with a freshman who soaks it all up.

scenarios.title: The Bad Film Session
scenarios.text: In the team film session, the coaches freeze on a kickoff return that went for a long gain last week. The coverage unit is getting chewed out, and the room goes quiet, waiting to see who speaks up.

choices.label: Own it out loud
choices.result: You say kickoffs start with you, and you'll work on hang time and placement so the coverage has a chance. The room relaxes, and a couple of guys on the coverage unit nod at you afterward.

choices.label: Stay quiet and take notes
choices.result: You keep your head down and write down what the coaches say. You learn exactly what to fix, though a few coverage guys look annoyed that you didn't say anything.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Teammate
scenarios.text: Jonah Pike, the quarterback you welcomed last year, shows up at your summer kicking session with a ball bag. He says he's been learning to hold, just in case, and asks if you want to try a few together.

choices.label: Work with him all summer
choices.result: You spend three mornings a week on snaps and spots. By August Jonah's holds are clean, you're trading jokes on every rep, and you have a real friend on the offense.

choices.label: Keep your routine solo
choices.result: You tell him thanks, but you work best alone and already have a holder. He shrugs it off, and the two of you stay friendly without getting much closer.

scenarios.title: The Academic Scholarship
scenarios.text: Your guidance counselor pulls you aside: your grades put you in range for a state academic scholarship, but only if you keep them up and take the harder math class next semester. It would cover college no matter what happens with football.

choices.label: Sign up for the harder class
choices.result: You switch into the advanced class and start a study plan around practice. Some nights are long, but the counselor puts your name on the scholarship list.

choices.label: Keep your focus on football
choices.result: You thank the counselor and stay in your current classes. Your schedule stays manageable, and you keep betting on your leg.

scenarios.title: The Community Recognition
scenarios.text: The organizers of the youth sports field project remember that you stayed for the full setup morning a couple of years ago. They invite you back to help at a community event, and a few people mention how much that earlier effort meant.

choices.label: Accept the recognition
choices.result: You thank the organizers and share how good it feels to see the field full of young players. You spend more time talking with families than you planned, but the community connection grows.

choices.label: Get back to helping
choices.result: You thank them briefly and return to setting up equipment, keeping the focus on the kids and the event. You avoid the attention and get useful work done, though you miss a chance to build those community connections.

scenarios.title: The Former College Kicker
scenarios.text: A guy who kicked at a college a few years back is home for the summer and offers to work with a few local kickers. After one session he says you have a good leg but no real plan.

choices.label: Fix the one thing he saw
choices.result: You spend every session on the hitch he spotted in your plant step. By the end of the summer it's gone, and your kicks fly straighter than they ever have.

choices.label: Build a full program with him
choices.result: You sketch out a season-long plan together: lifting, flexibility, kicking volume and rest days. It's a lot to keep up with, but for the first time your training has a shape.

scenarios.title: The Student Leader
scenarios.text: The student leadership program gives your group a real project: organize the spring food drive for the whole district. Everyone looks at you to run it, since you handled the committee last year.

choices.label: Take the lead
choices.result: You set deadlines, split the team into routes and spend two weekends sorting cans in the gym. The drive breaks the school record, and the principal reads your name at the assembly.

choices.label: Help, but let someone else run it
choices.result: You volunteer for a route and leave the planning to another student. The drive goes fine, and you keep your weekends for kicking.

scenarios.title: The Rival's Private Message
