scenarios.text: Late on a school night, Jonah Pike sends you a private message. College recruiters have started calling him, his dad keeps asking about offers, and he admits he can't sleep. Whatever's been between you two, he says you're the only one who'd get it.

choices.label: Tell him how you handle it
choices.result: You write back for an hour about your own routine: one call a night, no checking offers before a game, and what you tell your family. He says it's the first time he's felt normal in weeks.

choices.label: Use it to get in his head
choices.result: You reply that big-time recruiters watch everything and one bad game can end it. He goes quiet, and the next day at practice he looks rattled. You feel sharp for a day, then mostly guilty.

scenarios.title: The Recruiting Video Deadline
scenarios.text: College coaches want highlight videos by the end of the month, and yours still isn't done. A teammate offers to make it look better than it really was, and {coach} has offered to look at any video before it goes out.

choices.label: Send only real kicks
choices.result: You cut a plain video of real game kicks, misses left out but nothing faked. It's shorter than you'd like, and it's all true.

choices.label: Let your teammate jazz it up
choices.result: Your teammate adds slow motion, music and a practice kick dressed up to look like a game. It looks incredible, and you hit send before you can second-guess it.

choices.label: Ask {coach} to review it first
choices.result: You bring your draft to {coach}, who cuts two clips and adds a short note with your stats. It takes an extra week, but it goes out with your coach's name behind it.

scenarios.title: The Screenshot
scenarios.text: The group chat you once challenged for mocking a teammate comes up again when someone shares an old screenshot. A few people start arguing about what happened, and you realize your earlier message is part of the conversation.

choices.label: Own what you said
choices.result: You explain why you spoke up and make it clear you still think the jokes crossed a line. The discussion gets uncomfortable, but your teammates know you haven't changed your position.

choices.label: Let the chat move on
choices.result: You don't respond and mute the conversation for the evening. You avoid another round of arguments, but people are left to guess whether you still stand by what you said.

scenarios.title: The Last Junior-Year Kick
scenarios.text: It's the last practice before the final game of junior year. {holder} wants to try a new way of spinning the laces on the hold, something they've practiced at home all week, and asks if you'll trust it on Friday.

choices.label: Trust the new hold
choices.result: You take twenty reps with the new spin and tell {holder} it's theirs on Friday. It feels strange for a few kicks, then it feels like it was always that way.

choices.label: Stick with the old hold for now
choices.result: You tell {holder} it's a good idea, but not for the last game of the year. You'll try it in the offseason. The holder nods, a little deflated.

scenarios.title: The New Coach
scenarios.text: The team hires a new special teams coordinator, Ray Hollis, who coached at a small college for ten years. On day one he wants to change your approach: a longer run-up and a different plant spot.

authoring.note: A new offensive coordinator or position coach joins the staff; the head coach ({coach}) stays the same person. The newcomer has no relationship value or placeholder: name them in the text and keep the name consistent. rel 'coach' still means the head coach.

choices.label: Give his changes a real try
choices.result: You spend two weeks rebuilding your approach the way Hollis wants. It feels awful at first, then a few kicks come off your foot better than ever.

choices.label: Push back and keep your approach
choices.result: You tell Hollis your approach got you here and you'd rather not change it senior year. He shrugs and says it's your leg, and {coach} watches the whole exchange.

scenarios.title: The Coach Wants an Explanation
scenarios.text: {coach} closes the office door and says something about the last few weeks doesn't add up. Before deciding anything, the coach wants the full story from you.

choices.label: Tell the whole truth
choices.result: You lay it all out, including the parts that make you look bad. It's an uncomfortable twenty minutes, but {coach} thanks you and says you can rebuild from here.

choices.label: Keep it vague
choices.result: You say it's been a weird stretch and promise it's handled. {coach} lets you go, but the look on the coach's face says the conversation isn't over.

scenarios.title: The Training Setback
scenarios.text: The first week of senior practice, your kicking hip flares up again, worse than before. The athletic trainer says it needs two weeks of real rest and rehab before you kick at full speed.

choices.label: Follow the rehab plan
choices.result: You do every stretch and band exercise and sit out full-speed kicking for two weeks. It's torture watching from the sideline, but you come back without the pain.

choices.label: Ease back in early
choices.result: You do most of the rehab but start kicking again after one week because you can't stand waiting. The hip mostly holds up, though it aches after every practice.

choices.label: Ignore the trainer
choices.result: You tape it, take the field the next day and kick through it. Your leg still has its pop, but the pain is back by the weekend and worse than ever.

scenarios.title: The Captain's Responsibility
scenarios.text: {coach} names you a special teams captain for your senior season. It comes with a say in the specialists' practice schedule, a spot at the coin toss, and the job of keeping the younger kickers on track.

choices.label: Lead by example
choices.result: You show up first, run the specialists' warmups and stay late with the freshmen. It costs you some of your own reps, but the unit starts to feel like yours.

choices.label: Make the role work for you
choices.result: You set the specialists' schedule around your own routine and hand the younger kickers the ball-shagging. Your practices get easier, but the freshmen stop asking you anything.

scenarios.title: The Holder's Big Moment
scenarios.text: The week of a big game, {holder} bobbles a few snaps at practice and teammates start joking about it. {holder} quietly asks whether you'd rather work with someone else.

choices.label: Settle in and trust them
choices.result: You give {holder} a calm nod and stay after practice to rep the hold until the ball goes down clean every time. By Thursday you're both locked in, and you make sure {holder} knows you'd want nobody else on the hold.

choices.label: Show your frustration
choices.result: You point out the bobbles in front of everyone. A few teammates agree with you, but {holder} goes quiet afterward, unsure whether you still trust them.

scenarios.title: The Final Evaluation
scenarios.text: {coach} runs a preseason evaluation for every senior: a timed kicking session, a film review and a one-on-one about your role this year. It's your last first impression.

choices.label: Let your work speak
choices.result: You hit your marks, own the misses on film and tell {coach} you'll take whatever role helps the team. The coach nods and says that's what a starter sounds like.

choices.label: Ask for a shot at the long kicks
choices.result: You tell {coach} you want the long field goals this year, not just the chip shots. The coach promises a look in practice, and you leave knowing you'll have to back it up.

scenarios.title: The Starting Job Is Yours
scenarios.text: You've earned the starting job, and {tyler} knows it. After practice, the two of you have a quiet moment near the equipment room; whatever your history has been, this change puts your relationship at a crossroads.

choices.label: Recognize what he pushed you to do
choices.result: You tell {tyler} that the competition helped you grow and that you respect the work he put in. The conversation is awkward at first, but it ends with a more honest understanding between you.

choices.label: Keep competing together
choices.result: You suggest continuing to train together, with clear goals and no promises about who comes out ahead. {tyler} considers it, and the familiar challenge gives both of you something to work toward.

scenarios.title: The Better Training Plan
scenarios.text: Halfway through senior season, you've been training on your own plan for months. {coach} watches a session and offers to rebuild it with you for the stretch run.

choices.label: Stick to your plan, all in
choices.result: You thank {coach} and double down on the plan you built: every lift, every rep, every rest day. It's your program, and you see it through.

choices.label: Rebuild it together
choices.result: You sit down with {coach} and rework the plan around the opponents left on the schedule. It means unlearning a few habits, but the coach is invested in it now too.

scenarios.title: The First Serious Recruiting Conversation
scenarios.text: A college coach sits down with you and {parent} after practice for the first real recruiting talk of your life. Before talking about a roster spot, the coach asks what you actually want from the next four years.

choices.label: Say what matters to you
choices.result: You talk about wanting to play, wanting a degree that means something, and wanting to stay close enough for {parent} to make games. The coach takes notes and says it helps to know who they're recruiting.

choices.label: Say what they want to hear
choices.result: You tell the coach you'd go anywhere, play any role and live in the weight room. The coach smiles and promises to stay in touch, though driving home you're not sure what you agreed to.

scenarios.title: The Favor Returned
scenarios.text: After a rough week, a teammate you once went out of your way to help catches you at your locker. That favor hasn't been forgotten, and now it's their turn: extra reps after practice, notes from the class you've been missing, whatever you need.

choices.label: Take them up on it
choices.result: You swallow your pride and say yes. For two weeks they stay late to work with you and walk you through the notes, and the rough patch starts to feel like a bump.

choices.label: Say you've got it handled
choices.result: You thank them and insist you're fine. You dig out of the hole on your own, slower than you'd like, and they don't offer again.

scenarios.title: The Family Disagreement About College
scenarios.text: {parent} has a stack of brochures on the kitchen table, all from schools within two hours of home. The program you're most excited about is eight hours away, and dinner keeps turning into a debate.

choices.label: Stand by your choice
choices.result: You tell {parent} this is your decision and you've thought it through. He goes quiet, then says he'll support you, but the next few dinners are short.

choices.label: Work out a deal together
choices.result: You sit down with {parent} and make a list that matters to both of you: distance, degree, playing time, cost. A couple of schools move up, a couple drop off, and the debates turn into planning.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Reference
scenarios.text: Someone in the community who has seen the effort you put in over time approaches you with an unexpected offer. They may be able to speak about your character and reliability, but they ask what kind of help you actually need.

choices.label: Accept their recommendation
choices.result: You thank them and accept the offer to serve as a reference. They point to the consistency they've seen from you, giving you a meaningful boost as you think about what comes next.

choices.label: Ask for specific guidance
choices.result: You explain what opportunity you're pursuing and ask what would make your application stronger. They agree to help you prepare, though you leave with a few more things to work on.

scenarios.title: The Second Recruiting Invitation
scenarios.text: Another college sends an official visit invitation, even though you've been talking seriously with a different program for months. Both coaches will hear about it either way.

choices.label: Tell both coaches the truth
choices.result: You call the coach you've been talking with and explain the invitation before deciding. The coach appreciates it, and you take the visit with nobody blindsided.

choices.label: Take the visit quietly
choices.result: You go on the visit without mentioning it to anyone. It's eye-opening to see another program up close, but you spend the drive home wondering how to bring it up.

scenarios.title: The Recruiter Checks the Film
scenarios.text: A college recruiter who has been following you calls with a question. What they've heard about you doesn't match the film they've seen, and they'd like you to explain the difference before their staff meeting.

choices.label: Send your real, full film
choices.result: You send every kick from the last season, misses included, with a short note. The recruiter thanks you for the honesty and says now they know what they're working with.

choices.label: Explain the context
choices.result: You walk through what happened: a windy night, a new holder, a stretch where your timing was off. The recruiter listens and says they'll keep watching.

choices.label: Stick to your story
choices.result: You insist the numbers are right and the film just doesn't show your best kicks. The call ends politely, but the recruiter stops returning your messages.

scenarios.title: The Younger Athlete Looks Up to You
scenarios.text: A younger athlete catches you after school and says they've noticed the way you carry yourself around the team and in the community. They ask how you stay steady when people are watching and others are counting on you.

choices.label: Take them under your wing
choices.result: You listen to their concerns and offer to check in with them from time to time. It takes some of your free time, but they leave encouraged and you realize your example matters.

choices.label: Give them a quick answer
choices.result: You share one practical piece of advice and encourage them to keep showing up for their work. You protect your afternoon, though the conversation ends before a real connection forms.

scenarios.title: A Family Thank-You
scenarios.text: As senior year gets busier, {parent} tells you how much your support has meant to the family over the years. The conversation turns to everything you've balanced together, and you realize there are things you haven't really said out loud.

choices.label: Talk openly with him
choices.result: You tell {parent} what the family's support has meant to you, and listen as he shares what he's been carrying too. The conversation takes time and brings up some difficult feelings, but you understand each other better.

choices.label: Keep things light tonight
choices.result: You thank {parent} and steer the conversation toward lighter topics. The evening stays comfortable and you get a chance to relax, though some important feelings remain unspoken.

scenarios.title: The Backup Plan Pays Off
scenarios.text: The letter from the state scholarship office arrives: your grades held up, and the academic scholarship is yours if you accept by the end of the month. A football offer may still come, or it may not.

choices.label: Accept the scholarship
choices.result: You sign the acceptance and mail it the same day. Whatever happens with football, college is paid for, and a weight you didn't know you were carrying lifts.

choices.label: Ask about combining aid
choices.result: You call the financial aid office to ask whether the scholarship can stack with an athletic offer. It takes three calls and a lot of forms, but you learn exactly what's possible.

scenarios.title: The Last Practice Together
scenarios.text: It's the last practice of your senior year. {coach} gathers the group while {holder} helps put away the equipment, and the familiar routine suddenly feels like something you'll miss; you have a chance to recognize the people who helped make it matter.

choices.label: Thank them for the support
choices.result: You thank {coach} for the guidance and {holder} for being someone you could count on. The words are simple, but both take them seriously, and the moment leaves the group feeling appreciated.

choices.label: Keep the moment to yourself
